notes.title: Introduction to data structures – revision sheet
notes.md:
## Definition and classification
- Data structure = organised way of storing data for efficient access and change; ADT = data + operations, implementation hidden
- **Primitive**: int, char, float, double, pointer (machine-level)
- **Non-primitive** → **linear** (array, stack, queue, linked list) | **non-linear** (tree, graph)
- Static (array, fixed size) vs dynamic (linked list); homogeneous (array) vs heterogeneous (structure)
- Choosing: hierarchy → tree; network → graph; undo/recursion → stack; printer jobs/BFS → queue
- Data → information; field → record → file

## Operations
Traversing, searching, inserting, deleting, sorting, merging

## Complexity
- Time / space as a function of input size n; best, average, worst case; time–space trade-off
- O (upper), Ω (lower), Θ (tight), o (strictly smaller); constants and lower terms dropped
- Growth: 1 < log n < √n < n < n log n < n² < n³ < 2ⁿ < n!
| Code pattern | Time |
|---|---|
| single loop to n | O(n) |
| i = i × 2 (or × 3) | O(log n) |
| i × i ≤ n | O(√n) |
| two nested loops to n | O(n²) |
| j from i to n (n = 4 → 10 steps) | O(n²) |
| three nested loops | O(n³) |
| naive Fibonacci | O(2ⁿ) |
- Recurrences: T(n−1) + 1 → n; T(n/2) + 1 → log n; 2T(n/2) + 1 → n; 2T(n/2) + n → n log n
- Algorithm properties (Knuth): finiteness, definiteness, input, output, effectiveness

notes.title: Introduction to data structures – detailed notes with worked examples
notes.md:
## Key terms
- **Data structure** – a way to organise data in memory so the needed operations are efficient
- **Abstract data type (ADT)** – what the operations do (interface), not how (implementation). Stack ADT: push, pop, peek, isEmpty
- **Algorithm** – finite, definite, effective steps with input and output (Knuth's five properties: finiteness, definiteness, input, output, effectiveness)

## Classification
| | Examples |
|---|---|
| Primitive | int, char, float, double, pointer, boolean |
| Linear (non-primitive) | array, linked list, stack, queue |
| Non-linear | tree, graph |
| Static | array (size fixed at compile time) |
| Dynamic | linked list, tree (grow at run time) |
| Homogeneous / heterogeneous | array / structure (record) |

## Counting steps – worked examples
| Code | Count | Order |
|---|---|---|
| `for (i = 0; i < n; i++) s++;` | n | O(n) |
| `for (i = 0; i < n; i++) for (j = 0; j < n; j++) s++;` | n² | O(n²) |
| `for (i = 0; i < n; i++) for (j = 0; j < i; j++) s++;` | n(n − 1)/2 | O(n²) |
| `for (i = 1; i < n; i *= 2) s++;` | ⌈log₂ n⌉ | O(log n) |
| `for (i = n; i > 0; i /= 2) for (j = 0; j < n; j++) s++;` | n log n | O(n log n) |
| `for (i = 1; i < n; i *= 2) for (j = 0; j < i; j++) s++;` | 1 + 2 + 4 + … < 2n | **O(n)** |
| `for (i = 1; i * i <= n; i++) s++;` | √n | O(√n) |
| `for (i = 2; i < n; i = i * i) s++;` | log log n | O(log log n) |
| Two separate (not nested) loops of n | 2n | O(n) |

## Asymptotic notation
- **O** upper bound (worst case usually), **Ω** lower bound, **Θ** tight bound; little-o / little-ω strict
- Drop constants and lower terms: 3n² + 10n log n + 500 = **O(n²)**
- Growth order: 1 < log n < √n < n < n log n < n² < n³ < 2ⁿ < n! < nⁿ
- log bases do not matter in O (log₂ n and log₁₀ n differ by a constant)

## Recurrences (divide and conquer)
| Recurrence | Solution | Algorithm |
|---|---|---|
| T(n) = T(n/2) + 1 | O(log n) | binary search |
| T(n) = T(n − 1) + 1 | O(n) | linear recursion, factorial |
| T(n) = T(n − 1) + n | O(n²) | selection sort recursion, quicksort worst |
| T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n | O(n log n) | merge sort, quicksort best |
| T(n) = 2T(n/2) + 1 | O(n) | tree traversal |
| T(n) = 2T(n − 1) + 1 | O(2ⁿ) | Tower of Hanoi (2ⁿ − 1 moves) |
**Master theorem** for T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n), compare f(n) with n^(log_b a):
1. f smaller → Θ(n^(log_b a)) — e.g. 8T(n/2) + n² → n³
2. equal → Θ(n^(log_b a) · log n) — e.g. 2T(n/2) + n → n log n
3. f larger → Θ(f(n)) — e.g. 2T(n/2) + n² → n²

## Space complexity
- Fixed part (code, constants) + variable part (input-dependent, recursion stack)
- Recursive factorial uses O(n) stack; iterative O(1); merge sort needs O(n) extra; quicksort O(log n) stack on average
- **Time–space trade-off**: e.g. a lookup table (more memory, less time)

## Operations on any data structure
Traversing, searching, inserting, deleting, sorting, merging

## Traps
- O(n) "is also" O(n²) (upper bound) – exams ask for the tightest
- Best case of linear search is O(1), not O(n)
- Amortised O(1) (dynamic array append) ≠ worst-case O(1)

notes.title: KRIES syllabus word by word – Introduction to data structures
notes.md:
> **Syllabus:** Definition, classification of data structures, operations on data structures, introduction to time and space complexity

### Definition (of a data structure)
- **Means:** a way of organising and storing data in memory so that it can be used efficiently.
- **Key facts:** data structure + algorithm = program (Niklaus Wirth); choice depends on the operations needed; an **ADT** states the operations, the data structure implements them.
- **Example:** a phone contact list kept sorted (array) for binary search, or as a linked list for easy insertion.
- **Exam point:** a data structure is about **organisation**, an algorithm about **steps**.

### Classification of data structures
- **Means:** grouping by nature.
- **Key facts:** **primitive** (int, char, float, pointer) vs **non-primitive**; non-primitive → **linear** (array, stack, queue, linked list – elements in sequence) and **non-linear** (tree, graph – hierarchy/network); **static** (fixed size – array) vs **dynamic** (grows – linked list); homogeneous vs heterogeneous.
- **Example:** family tree → tree; road map → graph; plates pile → stack; ticket line → queue.
- **Exam point:** stack and queue are **linear**; tree and graph are **non-linear**.

### Operations on data structures
- **Means:** what we do with the stored data.
- **Key facts:** **traversing** (visit each element once), **searching** (find an element), **inserting**, **deleting**, **sorting** (arrange in order), **merging** (combine two sorted lists); also create, update, destroy.
- **Example:** printing every student's marks = traversal.
- **Exam point:** "visiting every element exactly once" = **traversal**.

### Introduction to time complexity
- **Means:** how the running time grows with input size n.
- **Key facts:** counted in basic operations, expressed with **Big-O** (upper bound), Ω (lower), Θ (tight); best, average, worst case; order: 1 < log n < n < n log n < n² < 2ⁿ < n!
- **Example:** one loop over n → O(n); two nested loops → O(n²); halving each step → O(log n).
- **Exam point:** linear search worst case O(n), binary search O(log n).

### Introduction to space complexity
- **Means:** how much memory an algorithm needs as n grows.
- **Key facts:** fixed part (code, constants, simple variables) + variable part (arrays sized by n, **recursion stack**); auxiliary space = extra space beyond the input.
- **Example:** iterative factorial O(1) space; recursive factorial O(n) (n stack frames); merge sort O(n) extra.
- **Exam point:** time–space trade-off – using more memory (e.g. a lookup table) to save time.

notes.md:
| Code | Count | Order |
|---|---|---|
| `for (i = 0; i < n; i++) for (j = 0; j < n; j++) x++;` | n² | O(n²) |
| `for (i = 0; i < n; i++) for (j = i; j < n; j++) x++;` | n(n + 1)/2 | O(n²) |
| `for (i = 1; i < n; i = i * 2) x++;` | ⌈log₂ n⌉ | O(log n) |
| `for (i = n; i > 0; i = i / 2) for (j = 0; j < i; j++) x++;` | n + n/2 + … < 2n | **O(n)** |
| `for (i = 0; i < n; i++) for (j = 1; j < n; j *= 2) x++;` | n log n | O(n log n) |
| `for (i = 1; i * i <= n; i++) x++;` | √n | O(√n) |
| `for (i = 0; i < n; i++); for (j = 0; j < n; j++) x++;` | 2n (two separate loops) | O(n) |
| `int f(int n) { return n <= 1 ? 1 : f(n - 1) + f(n - 1); }` | 2ⁿ calls | O(2ⁿ) |
| `int g(int n) { return n <= 1 ? 1 : g(n / 2) + 1; }` | log n calls | O(log n) |

### Q. Which grows fastest?
n log n, n¹·⁵, 2ⁿ, n! → order n log n < n¹·⁵ < 2ⁿ < n!; log n² = 2 log n = O(log n); 2ⁿ⁺¹ = O(2ⁿ) but 4ⁿ ≠ O(2ⁿ).

### Q. Space
Recursive sum of an array of n elements uses O(n) stack; iterative O(1); merge sort O(n) extra; quick sort O(log n) average stack.

notes.title: Primitive data structures – revision sheet
notes.md:
## Integers
- 2's complement: n bits → −2ⁿ⁻¹ … 2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1 (8-bit −128…127; 32-bit ±2.1 × 10⁹); −5 = 11111011
- Unsigned 16-bit 0…65,535; unsigned arithmetic wraps (255 + 1 = 0 in 8 bits; 250 + 10 = 4)
- Operations: + − × / % (17 / 5 = 3, 17 % 5 = 2), comparison, bitwise
- Little-endian stores the least significant byte first (0x12345678 → 78 56 34 12)

## Characters
- ASCII 7-bit ('A' 65 = 01000001, 'a' 97, '0' 48, space 32); Unicode/UTF-8 for Kannada etc.
- Arithmetic on codes: 'a' + 2 = 'c'; c − '0' gives a digit's value; lowercase − 32 = uppercase

## Floating point
- IEEE 754: float 1 + 8 + 23 (≈ 7 digits), double 1 + 11 + 52 (≈ 15–16 digits); normalized mantissa starts with 1
- 0.1 is not exact (0.5 is) – never compare floats with ==; store money as integer paise

## Strings
- C: char array ending in '\0' ("KEA" = 4 bytes; sizeof("") = 1); Pascal: length byte
- Representations: fixed-length, variable-length (terminator or length), linked
- Pointer idioms: length `while (*p) p++; return p − s;`; copy `while ((*d++ = *s++));`; reverse with two pointers (⌊n/2⌋ swaps); atoi `n = n*10 + (*p − '0')`
- Library: strlen, strcpy, strncpy, strcat (O(len1 + len2)), strcmp (code order: 'Z' < 'a'), strchr, strstr, strtok
- Array of char pointers saves space for ragged strings; sort by swapping pointers; compare with strcmp, not ==

notes.md:
## What "primitive" means
Basic types operated on directly by machine instructions: **integer, real (float/double), character, boolean, pointer**. Non-primitive structures (arrays, lists, trees) are built from them.

## Integers
- Unsigned n bits: 0 … 2ⁿ − 1 (8 bits: 0 … 255)
- **Two's complement** signed n bits: −2ⁿ⁻¹ … 2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1 (8 bits: −128 … 127; 16 bits: −32,768 … 32,767)
- Negate: invert all bits and add 1 → −5 in 8 bits: 00000101 → 11111010 → **11111011**
- Other forms: sign-magnitude and one's complement (both have two zeros, +0 and −0)
- Overflow: 127 + 1 in 8-bit signed wraps to −128

## Number-system conversions (worked)
- 156 → binary: 156 = 128 + 16 + 8 + 4 → **10011100** → octal (groups of 3 from right: 010 011 100) **234** → hex (groups of 4: 1001 1100) **9C**
- 0x2F = 2 × 16 + 15 = **47**; 0o17 = 15; 1011.101₂ = 11.625
- Decimal fraction 0.375 → ×2: 0.75 (0), 1.5 (1), 1.0 (1) → **0.011₂**

## Real numbers – IEEE 754
| Format | Sign | Exponent | Mantissa | Bias |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Single (float, 32-bit) | 1 | 8 | 23 | **127** |
| Double (64-bit) | 1 | 11 | 52 | 1023 |
Worked: **5.75** = 101.11₂ = 1.0111 × 2² → sign 0, exponent 2 + 127 = 129 = 10000001, mantissa 0111000… → **0x40B80000**
Worked: **−13.25** = −1101.01₂ = −1.10101 × 2³ → sign 1, exponent 130 = 10000010 → **0xC1540000**
- Value = (−1)ˢ × 1.mantissa × 2^(exponent − bias); exponent all 1s = infinity/NaN; all 0s = zero/denormal
- 0.1 cannot be stored exactly → never compare floats with ==

## Characters
- ASCII 7-bit (128 codes); 'A' = 65, 'a' = 97, '0' = 48, space = 32, '\n' = 10; upper ↔ lower differ by 32
- Digit value: `c − '0'`; EBCDIC (IBM), **Unicode** (UTF-8 1–4 bytes, UTF-16) for all scripts including Kannada

## Boolean and pointer
- Boolean: true/false; in C any non-zero is true (`_Bool` / `<stdbool.h>` since C99)
- Pointer: stores an address; size depends on the machine (4 bytes on 32-bit, 8 on 64-bit), not on the type pointed to

## Operations on primitive types
Create (declare), select (access), update (assign), destroy (go out of scope); arithmetic, logical, relational, bitwise

## Traps
- Range of a signed 8-bit number is −128 … **127** (not 128)
- Hex digit = 4 bits, octal digit = 3 bits
- IEEE single bias is 127, double bias is 1023
- sizeof(char) is always 1 in C

notes.title: KRIES syllabus word by word – Primitive data structures
notes.md:
> **Syllabus:** Integer, character, float, strings – memory representation and primitive operations; string manipulation using pointers

### Integer
- **Means:** whole numbers, stored in binary.
- **Key facts:** n bits unsigned 0 … 2ⁿ − 1; signed uses **two's complement**: −2ⁿ⁻¹ … 2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1 (int 32-bit: −2,147,483,648 … 2,147,483,647); −5 in 8 bits = 11111011.
- **Example:** 13 = 00001101.
- **Exam point:** overflow wraps around (unsigned); signed overflow is undefined in C.

### Character
- **Means:** a single symbol stored as a small integer code.
- **Key facts:** **ASCII** 7-bit (128 codes, stored in 1 byte): 'A' 65, 'a' 97, '0' 48, space 32; **Unicode** for all scripts (UTF-8, UTF-16; Java char = 2 bytes).
- **Example:** `'a' - 'A'` = 32; `'7' - '0'` = 7.
- **Exam point:** upper ↔ lower case differ by 32 (bit 5).

### Float
- **Means:** real numbers in **IEEE 754** floating point.
- **Key facts:** single (32-bit): 1 sign + 8 exponent (bias 127) + 23 mantissa; double (64-bit): 1 + 11 (bias 1023) + 52; value = (−1)ˢ × 1.m × 2^(e − bias).
- **Example:** 5.75 = 1.0111 × 2² → 0 10000001 0111000… = 0x40B80000.
- **Exam point:** 0.1 can't be stored exactly – never compare floats with `==`.

### Strings
- **Means:** a sequence of characters; in C a char array ending with `'\0'`.
- **Key facts:** length n needs n + 1 bytes; stored in contiguous memory; literals are read-only.
- **Example:** "DATA" → 'D' 'A' 'T' 'A' '\0' (5 bytes).
- **Exam point:** `strlen` excludes `'\0'`, `sizeof` of the array includes it.

### Memory representation
- **Means:** how each type is laid out in bytes.
- **Key facts:** int 4 bytes (little-endian on x86: lowest byte at the lowest address), char 1, float 4, double 8, pointer 8 (64-bit); arrays/strings contiguous.
- **Example:** int 0x12345678 at address 100 on little-endian: 100 → 78, 101 → 56, 102 → 34, 103 → 12.
- **Exam point:** big-endian stores the **most** significant byte first (network byte order).

### Primitive operations
- **Means:** basic operations directly supported on primitive types.
- **Key facts:** create (declare), select/access, update (assign), destroy; arithmetic, relational, logical, bitwise operations; type conversion.
- **Example:** `int x = 5; x = x * 2;` → create, access, update.
- **Exam point:** primitive types are operated on by **machine instructions** directly.

### String manipulation using pointers
- **Means:** walking through a string with a `char *` instead of indexes.
- **Key facts:** loop `while (*p) p++;` stops at `'\0'`; length = p − s; copy `while ((*d++ = *s++));`; compare character by character.
- **Example:** `int len(char *s) { char *p = s; while (*p) p++; return p - s; }` → len("KRIES") = 5.
- **Exam point:** `*p++` reads then moves; reverse a string with two pointers swapping from both ends.

notes.title: Arrays – revision sheet
notes.md:
## Storage representation
- 1-D: Loc(A[i]) = Base + w × (i − LB); number of elements = UB − LB + 1
- 2-D (m × n): row-major Loc = Base + w × (n × (i − LB₁) + (j − LB₂)); column-major Base + w × (m × (j − LB₂) + (i − LB₁))
  - char a[100][100] at 0 → a[40][50] = 4050; A[5][4], w = 4, base 100 → A[3][2] = 156 (row) / 152 (column)
- 3-D: A[1][2][3] of A[2][3][4] = 1·12 + 2·4 + 3 = 23 elements from the base
- Special matrices: lower triangular n(n + 1)/2 (index i(i+1)/2 + j), tridiagonal 3n − 2, diagonal n; sparse → triplets (header + one row per non-zero)

## Insertion and deletion (n elements)
- Insert at pos: check overflow; shift a[n−1]…a[pos] right (from the end); place; n++ → O(n) (front worst, end O(1))
- Delete at pos: shift a[pos+1]…a[n−1] left; n−− → n − pos − 1 moves; unordered delete: copy last element in, O(1)
- Insert into a sorted array: find the position, then shift

## Advantages / disadvantages
| Advantages | Disadvantages |
|---|---|
| O(1) random access | fixed size (overflow or waste) |
| no pointer overhead | O(n) insert/delete in the middle |
| simple, cache-friendly | needs one contiguous block |
- Dynamic arrays grow by doubling (amortised O(1) append); parallel arrays

notes.title: Arrays in data structures – detailed notes with worked examples
notes.md:
## Properties
- Contiguous memory, same type, random access by index in **O(1)**
- Fixed size; insertion/deletion in the middle needs shifting → O(n)

## Address formulas (w = bytes per element)
- 1-D, lower bound LB: **base + (i − LB) × w**
- 2-D row-major: **base + ((i − LR) × N + (j − LC)) × w** (N = number of columns)
- 2-D column-major: **base + ((j − LC) × M + (i − LR)) × w** (M = number of rows)
- Number of elements in A[l₁..u₁][l₂..u₂] = (u₁ − l₁ + 1)(u₂ − l₂ + 1)

Worked examples
1. A[1..10], base 2000, w = 4 → A[7] = 2000 + (7 − 1) × 4 = **2024**
2. `int a[3][4]`, base 1000, w = 4 → a[2][1] = 1000 + (2 × 4 + 1) × 4 = **1036**
3. A[−2..5][3..8], base 500, w = 2 → 8 × 6 = 48 elements; A[1][5]: row-major 500 + (3 × 6 + 2) × 2 = **540**; column-major 500 + (2 × 8 + 3) × 2 = **538**
4. 3-D A[L][M][N] row-major: base + ((i × M + j) × N + k) × w

## Operations with cost
| Operation | Cost | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Access a[i] | O(1) | address formula |
| Search (unsorted) | O(n) | linear search |
| Search (sorted) | O(log n) | binary search |
| Insert at position k | O(n) | shift a[k … n−1] right, from the **end** backwards |
| Delete at position k | O(n) | shift a[k+1 … n−1] left |
| Insert at end | O(1) | if space |

Insert 25 at index 2 of [10, 20, 30, 40]: move 40 → a[4], 30 → a[3], put 25 → **[10, 20, 25, 30, 40]** (2 shifts)

## Special matrices
- **Sparse matrix**: mostly zeros → store (row, col, value) **triplets**; first row of the triplet table often holds (rows, cols, count)
  - 4 × 5 matrix with 3 non-zero values → triplet table of 4 rows × 3 columns
- **Lower triangular** n × n: n(n + 1)/2 non-zero elements; row-major index of (i, j), 1-based, i ≥ j: **i(i − 1)/2 + (j − 1)**
- Upper triangular: also n(n + 1)/2; **tridiagonal**: 3n − 2 elements; diagonal: n
- Symmetric matrix: store only one triangle

## Array vs linked list
| | Array | Linked list |
|---|---|---|
| Memory | contiguous | scattered nodes |
| Size | fixed | dynamic |
| Access i-th | O(1) | O(n) |
| Insert/delete at front | O(n) | O(1) |
| Extra memory | none | a pointer per node |
| Cache friendly | yes | no |

## Uses
Lookup tables, matrices, implementing stacks/queues/heaps/hash tables, strings, polynomials (coefficient arrays)

## Traps
- C arrays are row-major; Fortran/MATLAB column-major
- For row-major the **column count** appears in the formula; for column-major the **row count**
- Upper bound minus lower bound **plus one** = number of elements

notes.title: KRIES syllabus word by word – Arrays
notes.md:
> **Syllabus:** Storage representation of 1-D and 2-D arrays, insertion and deletion on 1-D arrays, advantages and disadvantages of arrays

### Storage representation of 1-D arrays
- **Means:** how a 1-D array sits in memory – one block of consecutive cells.
- **Key facts:** Loc(A[i]) = Base + w × (i − LB); number of elements = UB − LB + 1.
- **Example:** A[1..20], base 500, w = 2 → A[12] = 500 + 2 × 11 = **522**.
- **Exam point:** random access in **O(1)** because of this formula.

### Storage representation of 2-D arrays
- **Means:** mapping rows × columns onto linear memory.
- **Key facts:** **row-major** (C): Base + w × [(i − LR) × N + (j − LC)]; **column-major** (Fortran): Base + w × [(j − LC) × M + (i − LR)]; M rows, N columns.
- **Example:** A[3][4], base 1000, w = 4, A[2][1]: row-major 1000 + 4 × 9 = **1036**; column-major 1000 + 4 × (1 × 3 + 2) = **1020**.
- **Exam point:** row-major uses the column count, column-major the row count.

### Insertion on 1-D arrays
- **Means:** adding an element at position k.
- **Key facts:** check space; shift A[n−1] … A[k] one place right (start from the **end**); put the item; n++. Cost O(n) (worst at the front), O(1) at the end.
- **Example:** [10, 20, 30, 40], insert 25 at index 2 → [10, 20, 25, 30, 40] (2 shifts).
- **Exam point:** shifting from the front would overwrite data.

### Deletion on 1-D arrays
- **Means:** removing the element at position k.
- **Key facts:** save A[k]; shift A[k+1] … A[n−1] one place left; n−−. Cost O(n).
- **Example:** [10, 20, 30, 40] delete index 1 → [10, 30, 40].
- **Exam point:** average shifts ≈ n/2 for insertion or deletion.

### Advantages of arrays
- **Means:** why arrays are used.
- **Key facts:** O(1) random access by index; simple; no pointer overhead; cache-friendly (contiguous); easy to implement stacks, queues, heaps, matrices.
- **Example:** marks of 60 students in `int m[60]`.
- **Exam point:** best when size is known and access is by position.

### Disadvantages of arrays
- **Means:** limits of arrays.
- **Key facts:** fixed size (waste or overflow); insertion/deletion costly (shifting); needs one contiguous block; homogeneous only.
- **Example:** declaring 1000 cells for 10 values wastes memory.
- **Exam point:** these are solved by **linked lists**.

notes.title: Linked lists – revision sheet
notes.md:
## Basics
- Node = data + pointer(s): `struct node { int data; struct node *next; };` (self-referential)
- Create: `t = (struct node *) malloc(sizeof(struct node));` (NULL → overflow); release: `free(t)`; AVAIL list (Lipschutz)
- Empty: head == NULL; deleting from empty = underflow; forgetting free = memory leak; using freed node = dangling pointer

## Operations (singly, head pointer only)
| Operation | Code | Time |
|---|---|---|
| insert at front | t->next = head; head = t | O(1) |
| insert after p | t->next = p->next; p->next = t | O(1) |
| insert at end | traverse (O(1) with tail) | O(n) |
| delete first | tmp = head; head = head->next; free(tmp) | O(1) |
| delete last | find second-last | O(n) |
| search / k-th element | traverse | O(n) |
- Reverse iteratively O(n); middle by slow/fast pointers; cycle by Floyd's method; merge sorted lists O(m + n)

## Variants
- Circular: last → first, no NULL; traverse with do … while (p != head); round-robin, Josephus; front insert O(1) with a last pointer
- Doubly (two-way): prev + data + next (3 fields, 2n pointers); delete p: p->prev->next = p->next; p->next->prev = p->prev
- Header lists: grounded (last → NULL) or circular (last → header)
- Uses: polynomials (coefficient, exponent nodes), stacks and queues, hash chaining, sparse matrices
- Prefer lists for frequent insert/delete and unknown size; arrays for random access

notes.title: Linked lists – detailed notes with worked examples
notes.md:
## Node and kinds
```c
struct node { int data; struct node *next; };
```
| Kind | Links | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Singly | next | one direction |
| **Doubly** | prev + next | both directions; delete a given node in O(1) |
| **Circular** | last → first | no NULL; any node can be the start; round-robin |
| Circular doubly | both ways, closed | |
| Header list | dummy first node | simplifies insert/delete |

## Core operations (singly)
```c
/* insert at beginning – O(1) */
t = malloc(sizeof *t); t->data = x; t->next = head; head = t;

/* insert at end – O(n) without a tail pointer */
t->next = NULL; if (!head) head = t; else { p = head; while (p->next) p = p->next; p->next = t; }

/* insert after node p */
t->next = p->next; p->next = t;          /* order matters – reversing these loses the rest */

/* delete first */
t = head; head = head->next; free(t);

/* delete the node after p */
t = p->next; p->next = t->next; free(t);

/* traverse / count */
for (p = head, n = 0; p; p = p->next) n++;
```

## Reverse a list (three pointers) – trace on 1 → 2 → 3
```c
prev = NULL; cur = head;
while (cur) { nxt = cur->next; cur->next = prev; prev = cur; cur = nxt; }
head = prev;
```
| Step | prev | cur | list so far |
|---|---|---|---|
| start | NULL | 1 | |
| 1 | 1 | 2 | 1 → NULL |
| 2 | 2 | 3 | 2 → 1 → NULL |
| 3 | 3 | NULL | 3 → 2 → 1 → NULL |

## Two-pointer tricks
- **Middle**: slow moves 1, fast moves 2; when fast reaches the end, slow is in the middle
- **Loop detection (Floyd)**: if slow and fast ever meet there is a cycle; O(n) time, O(1) space
- **k-th from end**: move one pointer k ahead, then move both
- Merge two sorted lists in O(m + n)

## Doubly linked insertion (after p)
```c
t->next = p->next; t->prev = p;
if (p->next) p->next->prev = t;
p->next = t;
```
Deleting node q: `q->prev->next = q->next; q->next->prev = q->prev; free(q);` (check the ends)

## Costs
| Operation | Singly | Doubly |
|---|---|---|
| Insert/delete at head | O(1) | O(1) |
| Insert at tail | O(n) (O(1) with tail pointer) | O(1) with tail |
| Delete a given node | O(n) (need previous) | **O(1)** |
| Search / access k-th | O(n) | O(n) |
- Binary search is not efficient on a linked list (no random access)

## Applications
Polynomials (coefficient, exponent, next) – adding two polynomials merges by exponent; sparse matrices; stacks and queues; adjacency lists of graphs; undo history; music playlists (circular); memory free lists

## Traps
- Always check for an empty list (head == NULL)
- Losing the head pointer loses the whole list (memory leak)
- In a circular list the loop condition is `p->next != head`, not `p != NULL`
- A doubly linked node needs **two** pointer fields → more memory

notes.title: KRIES syllabus word by word – Linked lists
notes.md:
> **Syllabus:** Pointers, dynamic memory allocation, singly linked lists and their operations, insertion and deletion of a node; circular and doubly linked lists

### Pointers
- **Means:** variables holding addresses – the "links" of a linked list.
- **Key facts:** each node holds data + pointer to the next node; `head` points to the first node; last node's next = NULL.
- **Example:** `struct node { int data; struct node *next; };`
- **Exam point:** losing `head` loses the whole list.

### Dynamic memory allocation
- **Means:** getting memory at run time from the **heap**.
- **Key facts:** `malloc(size)` (garbage), `calloc(n, size)` (zeroed), `realloc`, `free`; returns NULL on failure; forgetting free → memory leak.
- **Example:** `struct node *t = malloc(sizeof(struct node));`
- **Exam point:** this is what lets a linked list grow and shrink.

### Singly linked lists
- **Means:** nodes linked in one direction (next only).
- **Key facts:** access only from head; traversal O(n); no random access; extra memory per node for one pointer.
- **Example:** head → 10 → 20 → 30 → NULL.
- **Exam point:** to delete a node you need its **previous** node.

### Operations (on singly linked lists)
- **Means:** creation, traversal, search, count, insertion, deletion, reversal, concatenation.
- **Key facts:** traverse `for (p = head; p != NULL; p = p->next)`; search O(n); reverse with three pointers (prev, cur, next).
- **Example:** counting nodes of the list above → 3.
- **Exam point:** middle node = slow/fast pointer method.

### Insertion of a node
- **Means:** adding a node at the beginning, end or after a given node.
- **Key facts:** beginning: `t->next = head; head = t;` (O(1)); end: walk to last, `last->next = t; t->next = NULL;` (O(n)); after p: `t->next = p->next; p->next = t;` (this order!).
- **Example:** insert 15 after 10 in 10 → 20 → 10 → 15 → 20.
- **Exam point:** swapping the two lines of "insert after" breaks the list.

### Deletion of a node
- **Means:** unlinking and freeing a node.
- **Key facts:** first: `t = head; head = head->next; free(t);`; after p: `t = p->next; p->next = t->next; free(t);`; check empty list (underflow).
- **Example:** delete 20 from 10 → 20 → 30 → 10 → 30.
- **Exam point:** free the node **after** relinking.

### Circular linked lists
- **Means:** the last node points back to the first (no NULL).
- **Key facts:** any node can start a traversal; stop when you come back to the start (`p->next != head`); often a tail pointer is kept (tail->next = head) → insert at both ends in O(1).
- **Example:** round-robin CPU scheduling, multiplayer turns.
- **Exam point:** using `p != NULL` as the stop test loops forever.

### Doubly linked lists
- **Means:** each node has **prev** and **next** pointers.
- **Key facts:** traverse both ways; delete a given node in O(1); more memory (two pointers); insertion updates four links.
- **Example:** browser back/forward history, music playlist.
- **Exam point:** a node of a doubly linked list of ints on 64-bit: 4 + 8 + 8 = 20 → 24 bytes with padding.

notes.md:
## Concept and implementation
- LIFO; push, pop, peek/top, isEmpty, isFull – all O(1)
- Array: top = −1 empty, top == MAX − 1 full; push: a[++top] = x; pop: x = a[top--]; overflow / underflow
- Linked (top = head): push t->next = top; top = t; pop temp = top; top = top->next; free(temp)
- Two stacks in one array grow from opposite ends: full when top1 = top2 − 1
- Stack permutations of 1, 2, 3: 5 possible (3 1 2 impossible); of n: Catalan number

## Applications
- Recursion / function calls (activation records); stack overflow on infinite recursion
- Tower of Hanoi: n − 1 to spare, largest to target, n − 1 to target; 2ⁿ − 1 moves (6 discs = 63); odd n → first move smallest disc to target
- Bracket matching, HTML tags, reversing strings, decimal → binary, undo/redo (two stacks), DFS, browser back
- Infix → postfix: operands to output; '(' push; ')' pop to '('; operator: pop ops of ≥ precedence (not for right-associative ^), then push
  - (A + B) * C − D / E → A B + C * D E / −; A + B * C ^ D → A B C D ^ * +; A − B / (C * D ^ E) prefix → − A / B * C ^ D E
- Postfix evaluation: push operands; on operator pop right then left, push result
  - 5 6 2 + * 12 4 / − = 37; 8 2 / 3 * 4 + = 16; prefix + * A B − C D (2, 3, 4, 5) = 5

notes.title: Stacks – detailed notes with worked examples
notes.md:
## Infix → postfix, step by step: A + B * C − D
| Symbol | Action | Stack | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | output | | A |
| + | push | + | A |
| B | output | + | A B |
| * | higher than + → push | + * | A B |
| C | output | + * | A B C |
| − | pop * and + (≥ precedence), push − | − | A B C * + |
| D | output | − | A B C * + D |
| end | pop all | | **A B C * + D −** |
Rules: operand → output; `(` → push; `)` → pop until `(`; operator → pop while the top has **higher or equal** precedence (for right-associative `^` only higher), then push. Precedence: `^` > `* / %` > `+ −`.

More: (A + B) * (C − D) → **A B + C D − ***; A * (B + C) / D → **A B C + * D /**; A ^ B ^ C → **A B C ^ ^** (right-associative)

## Infix → prefix
Reverse the infix (swap brackets), convert to postfix, reverse the result.
(A + B) * C → **\* + A B C**; A + B * C → **+ A * B C**

## Evaluate postfix: 2 3 4 * + 5 −
| Symbol | Stack |
|---|---|
| 2 | 2 |
| 3 | 2 3 |
| 4 | 2 3 4 |
| * | 2 12 |
| + | 14 |
| 5 | 14 5 |
| − | **9** |
Pop the **right** operand first: for `a b −` the result is a − b. Prefix is evaluated from **right to left**.

## Stack permutations
- With push/pop of 1, 2, 3 in order, 5 output orders are possible; **3 1 2** is impossible (3 out first means 1 and 2 are stacked with 2 on top)
- Count for n = **Catalan number** C(2n, n)/(n + 1): 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, 132

## Array implementation (MAX = 5)
```c
int s[MAX], top = -1;
void push(int x) { if (top == MAX - 1) puts("Overflow"); else s[++top] = x; }
int pop(void)    { if (top == -1) { puts("Underflow"); return -1; } return s[top--]; }
```
Trace: push 10, 20, 30, pop, push 40 → stack 10 20 40, top = 2

## Recursion uses a stack
- Each call pushes an activation record (parameters, locals, return address)
- fact(3) → push fact(3), fact(2), fact(1) → pop with results 1, 2, 6
- Converting recursion to iteration = using an explicit stack

## Applications
Function calls, undo, browser back, balanced brackets `{[()]}`, expression conversion/evaluation, **DFS**, backtracking (maze, N-queens), decimal → binary (push remainders, pop to print: 13 → 1101), reversing a string, Tower of Hanoi (2ⁿ − 1 moves)

## Variants
- Two stacks in one array: grow from both ends; overflow when top1 + 1 == top2
- Stack with two queues; **min-stack** (extra stack of minimums) gives getMin in O(1)
- Linked stack: push/pop at the head, no overflow (until memory runs out)

## Traps
- Underflow = pop from an empty stack; overflow = push onto a full stack
- In postfix there are no brackets and no precedence rules are needed
- Stack is LIFO; recursion depth = maximum stack size

notes.title: KRIES syllabus word by word – Stacks
notes.md:
> **Syllabus:** Concepts, operations, sequential and linked implementation; applications – recursion, Tower of Hanoi, infix to postfix, evaluation of postfix

### Concepts
- **Means:** a linear list where insertion and deletion happen at **one end (top)** – **LIFO** (last in, first out).
- **Key facts:** top points to the last inserted element; empty when top = −1 (array).
- **Example:** pile of plates; undo in an editor.
- **Exam point:** push A, B, C → pop gives C first.

### Operations
- **Means:** push (insert), pop (remove), peek/top (look), isEmpty, isFull.
- **Key facts:** all O(1); **overflow** = push on full, **underflow** = pop on empty.
- **Example:** push 1, push 2, pop, push 3 → stack 1 3 (top 3).
- **Exam point:** possible pop orders of 1, 2, 3 (pushed in order) = 5; 3 1 2 is impossible.

### Sequential implementation
- **Means:** stack in an array.
- **Key facts:** `push: if (top == MAX-1) overflow; else s[++top] = x;` · `pop: if (top == -1) underflow; else x = s[top--];` – fixed size.
- **Example:** MAX = 3, push 4 items → 4th causes overflow.
- **Exam point:** full when top = MAX − 1.

### Linked implementation
- **Means:** stack as a linked list with top = head.
- **Key facts:** push = insert at head, pop = delete head, both O(1); no overflow until memory ends; extra pointer per node.
- **Example:** push 5: `t->data = 5; t->next = top; top = t;`
- **Exam point:** empty when top == NULL.

### Applications – recursion
- **Means:** every function call pushes an **activation record** (parameters, locals, return address) on the call stack.
- **Key facts:** return pops it; too deep → stack overflow; any recursion can be rewritten with an explicit stack.
- **Example:** fact(3) → frames fact(3), fact(2), fact(1) pushed, then popped with 1, 2, 6.
- **Exam point:** depth of recursion = maximum stack size used.

### Applications – Tower of Hanoi
- **Means:** move n discs from A to C using B; one disc at a time; never a bigger disc on a smaller one.
- **Key facts:** move n − 1 to B, largest to C, n − 1 to C; moves = **2ⁿ − 1** (3 discs = 7, 4 = 15, 64 = 2⁶⁴ − 1).
- **Example:** n = 2: A→B, A→C, B→C.
- **Exam point:** T(n) = 2T(n − 1) + 1 → O(2ⁿ).

### Applications – infix to postfix
- **Means:** converting `A + B * C` (operator between) to `A B C * +` (operator after).
- **Key facts:** operands go to output; `(` pushed; `)` pops until `(`; an operator pops operators of higher or equal precedence first (except right-associative `^`); end: pop all.
- **Example:** (A + B) * C → A B + C *; A + B * C − D → A B C * + D −.
- **Exam point:** postfix needs no brackets and no precedence rules.

### Applications – evaluation of postfix
- **Means:** computing a postfix expression with an operand stack.
- **Key facts:** operand → push; operator → pop **right** (first pop) and **left** (second pop), push left op right; answer = the last value.
- **Example:** 6 2 / 3 − 4 2 * + → 6/2 = 3, 3 − 3 = 0, 4 × 2 = 8, 0 + 8 = **8**.
- **Exam point:** for `a b −` the result is a − b, not b − a.

### Infix → postfix
| Infix | Postfix |
|---|---|
| A + B * C − D / E | **A B C * + D E / −** |
| (A + B) * (C − D) / E | **A B + C D − * E /** |
| A * (B + C * D) + E | **A B C D * + * E +** |
| A ^ B ^ C * D | **A B C ^ ^ D *** (^ is right-associative) |
| K + L − M * N + (O ^ P) * W / U / V * T + Q | **K L + M N * − O P ^ W * U / V / T * + Q +** |

### Infix → prefix
| Infix | Prefix |
|---|---|
| A + B * C − D / E | **− + A * B C / D E** |
| (A + B) * (C − D) / E | **/ * + A B − C D E** |
| A * (B + C * D) + E | **+ * A + B * C D E** |

### Evaluation
- Postfix **5 3 + 8 2 − *** → (5 + 3) × (8 − 2) = **48**
- Prefix **− + 7 * 4 5 + 2 0** (scan right to left) → (7 + 4 × 5) − (2 + 0) = **25**
- Postfix 6 2 3 + − 3 8 2 / + * 2 ^ 3 + → 6 − 5 = 1; 8/2 = 4; 3 + 4 = 7; 1 × 7 = 7; 7² = 49; 49 + 3 = **52**

### Stack states
Push 10, 20, 30; pop; push 40; pop; pop → output **30, 40, 20**; stack holds 10.

### Maximum stack size during conversion
For A + B * C − D the operator stack reaches size **2** (+ and *).

### Tower of Hanoi
5 discs → 2⁵ − 1 = **31** moves; the largest disc moves exactly once; the smallest disc moves 2ⁿ⁻¹ = 16 times.

notes.title: Queues – revision sheet
notes.md:
## Concept and implementation
- FIFO; enqueue at rear, dequeue at front; also front/peek, isEmpty, isFull
- Linear array: full when rear == MAX − 1 even if front cells are free (wasted space)
- Circular array: rear = (rear + 1) % N, front = (front + 1) % N; one empty slot → empty: front == rear, full: (rear + 1) % N == front, capacity N − 1 (or keep a count to use all N); count = (rear − front + N) % N
- Linked queue: front = head, rear = tail, both O(1); reset rear to NULL when empty
- Queue from two stacks (amortised O(1)); stack from two queues

## Variants
- Priority queue: ascending (min first) / descending (max first); same priority → FIFO; heap → O(log n) insert and delete (sorted list: O(n) insert, O(1) delete); one queue per level
- Deque: insert/delete at both ends; input-restricted (insert at one end, delete at both); output-restricted (insert at both, delete at one)

## Applications
CPU round-robin scheduling, printer spooling, keyboard buffers (circular), BFS, simulations (bank queue), Josephus problem, Dijkstra / Prim / Huffman (min priority queue), palindromes with a deque

notes.title: Queues – detailed notes with worked examples
notes.md:
## Linear queue (array)
- FIFO; insert at **rear**, delete at **front**
- Start front = rear = −1; enqueue: `if (rear == MAX − 1) overflow; if (front == −1) front = 0; q[++rear] = x;`
- Dequeue: `x = q[front]; if (front == rear) front = rear = −1; else front++;`
- Problem: after deletions the freed front cells cannot be reused → "full" even with space → **circular queue**

## Circular queue (size N = 5) – trace
- Enqueue: `rear = (rear + 1) % N`; dequeue: `front = (front + 1) % N`
- **Full**: `(rear + 1) % N == front`; **empty**: front == −1 (or with the "one empty slot" method: front == rear)
- Elements = (rear − front + N) % N + 1 (when not empty)
| Operation | front | rear | Contents |
|---|---|---|---|
| enqueue 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 | 0 | 4 | 10 20 30 40 50 (full) |
| dequeue, dequeue | 2 | 4 | 30 40 50 |
| enqueue 60 | 2 | **0** | 30 40 50 60 |
| enqueue 70 | 2 | 1 | 30 40 50 60 70 → (1 + 1) % 5 = 2 = front → **full** |

## Linked queue
- front = head, rear = tail; enqueue at tail O(1), dequeue at head O(1); no overflow until memory ends

## Deque (double-ended queue)
- Insert and delete at **both** ends
- **Input-restricted**: insert at one end only, delete at both; **output-restricted**: delete at one end only, insert at both
- Can act as both a stack and a queue

## Priority queue
- Each element has a priority; the highest (or lowest) priority leaves first
| Implementation | Insert | Delete-max |
|---|---|---|
| Unsorted array/list | O(1) | O(n) |
| Sorted array/list | O(n) | O(1) |
| **Binary heap** | **O(log n)** | **O(log n)** |
- Max-heap from [4, 10, 3, 5, 1] (heapify from the last internal node) → **[10, 5, 3, 4, 1]**

## Queue using two stacks
- Enqueue: push on S1. Dequeue: if S2 empty, pop everything from S1 into S2; pop S2 → amortised O(1)

## Applications
CPU scheduling (ready queue, round robin = circular queue), printer spooling, keyboard and I/O buffers, **BFS**, call-centre/ticket systems, Josephus problem (circular)

## Comparison
| | Stack | Queue |
|---|---|---|
| Order | LIFO | FIFO |
| Ends used | one (top) | two (front, rear) |
| Insert / delete | push / pop | enqueue / dequeue |
| Graph search | DFS | BFS |

## Traps
- Circular queue of size N stores N elements with a separate count/flag, or **N − 1** with the "one empty slot" rule – check the question
- Priority queue is not FIFO for different priorities (FIFO only among equal priorities)
- Rear pointer moves on insertion, front on deletion

notes.title: KRIES syllabus word by word – Queues
notes.md:
> **Syllabus:** Concepts, operations, sequential and linked implementation; circular queues, priority queues and deques; applications of queues

### Concepts
- **Means:** a linear list with insertion at the **rear** and deletion at the **front** – **FIFO** (first in, first out).
- **Key facts:** two pointers front and rear; empty when front = −1 (or front > rear).
- **Example:** people at a bus stop; print jobs.
- **Exam point:** enqueue A, B, C → dequeue gives A first.

### Operations
- **Means:** enqueue (insert at rear), dequeue (remove from front), peek/front, isEmpty, isFull.
- **Key facts:** all O(1); overflow on a full queue, underflow on an empty one.
- **Example:** enqueue 1, 2, 3; dequeue → 1 leaves; queue 2 3.
- **Exam point:** rear moves on insertion, front on deletion.

### Sequential implementation
- **Means:** queue in an array.
- **Key facts:** enqueue `if (rear == MAX-1) overflow; if (front == -1) front = 0; q[++rear] = x;`; dequeue `x = q[front++]` (reset both to −1 when it becomes empty).
- **Example:** MAX 5: insert 5 items, delete 2 → rear = 4 → "full" though 2 cells are free.
- **Exam point:** this wasted space is why **circular queues** exist.

### Linked implementation
- **Means:** queue as a linked list – front = head, rear = tail.
- **Key facts:** enqueue at tail, dequeue at head, both O(1); no fixed size.
- **Example:** enqueue: `rear->next = t; rear = t;`
- **Exam point:** when the last node is removed set rear = NULL too.

### Circular queues
- **Means:** array queue whose end wraps to the start.
- **Key facts:** rear = (rear + 1) % N; front = (front + 1) % N; full when (rear + 1) % N == front; count = (rear − front + N) % N + 1.
- **Example:** N = 5, front 2, rear 4 → enqueue goes to index 0.
- **Exam point:** reuses freed cells, so no false "full".

### Priority queues
- **Means:** each element has a priority; the highest priority is removed first (FIFO among equals).
- **Key facts:** ascending (smallest first) or descending; best implemented with a **heap** (insert and delete O(log n)); sorted list gives O(n) insert, O(1) delete.
- **Example:** hospital emergency room; CPU scheduling by priority.
- **Exam point:** a priority queue is not strictly FIFO.

### Deques
- **Means:** double-ended queue – insert and delete at **both** ends.
- **Key facts:** **input-restricted** (insert at one end, delete at both) and **output-restricted** (delete at one end, insert at both); can act as stack or queue.
- **Example:** browser history with limited size; sliding-window maximum.
- **Exam point:** pronounced "deck"; not the same as dequeue (the operation).

### Applications of queues
- **Means:** where FIFO order is needed.
- **Key facts:** CPU/printer scheduling, **BFS** of graphs, level-order tree traversal, keyboard and I/O buffers, call centres, round robin (circular), simulation of waiting lines, Josephus problem.
- **Example:** BFS from A visits neighbours in the order they were queued.
- **Exam point:** BFS uses a queue, DFS uses a stack.

### Q3. Queue using two stacks
enqueue 1, 2, 3 (push on S1) → dequeue: move 3, 2, 1 to S2 → pop **1** → enqueue 4 (S1) → dequeue pops **2** from S2.

### Q4. Priority queue (smaller number = higher priority)
Insert (A, 3), (B, 1), (C, 2), (D, 1) → delete order **B, D, C, A** (B before D – FIFO among equal priorities).

### Q5. Restricted deques (input 1, 2, 3, 4 in that order)
- **Input-restricted** (insert at the rear only, delete at both ends): 4 1 3 2 is **possible** (insert all, delete rear 4, front 1, rear 3, then 2); the only impossible orders are **4 2 1 3** and **4 2 3 1**
- **Output-restricted** (insert at both ends, delete at the front only): 3 1 2 4 is **possible** (insert 1, 2 at the rear, 3 at the front, delete 3, 1, 2, then insert and delete 4); the only impossible orders are **4 1 3 2** and **4 2 3 1**
- A plain stack allows 14 of the 24 orders; a plain queue only 1 (1 2 3 4)

notes.title: Binary trees – revision sheet
notes.md:
## Concepts
- Tree with n nodes has n − 1 edges; binary tree: at most 2 children; level i has ≤ 2ⁱ nodes; height h has ≤ 2^(h+1) − 1 nodes
- Full/strict (0 or 2 children): leaves = internal + 1; complete (filled level by level); skewed (height n − 1)
- Minimum height with n nodes ⌊log₂ n⌋ (23 nodes → 4)

## Representation
- Sequential (1-based): left 2i, right 2i + 1, parent ⌊i/2⌋; complete tree → n cells; skewed tree wastes space
- Linked: left | data | right; n nodes → n + 1 NULL pointers (threaded trees reuse them)

## Traversals
| Traversal | Order | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Preorder | root, left, right | prefix of expression tree |
| Inorder | left, root, right | sorted for a BST |
| Postorder | left, right, root | postfix |
| Level order | by levels | uses a queue |
- Inorder + preorder (or postorder) fixes the tree; preorder + postorder does not
- BST 40, 20, 60, 10, 30 → pre 40 20 10 30 60, in 10 20 30 40 60, post 10 30 20 60 40, level 40 20 60 10 30

## Insertion and deletion (BST)
- Insert: go left if smaller, right if larger, attach as a leaf
- Delete: leaf → remove; one child → link the child up; two children → replace by inorder successor (or predecessor)
- Search O(h): O(log n) balanced, O(n) skewed (sorted input)

notes.title: Binary trees – detailed notes with worked examples
notes.md:
## Terms
Root, parent, child, siblings, leaf (degree 0), internal node, **degree** (number of children), **level** (root = 0), **depth** (edges from root), **height** (edges on the longest root-to-leaf path; one-node tree = 0), subtree, ancestor/descendant, forest

## Properties of binary trees
- Maximum nodes at level l = **2ˡ**; in a tree of height h = **2ʰ⁺¹ − 1**
- Minimum height with n nodes = ⌈log₂(n + 1)⌉ − 1
- **n₀ = n₂ + 1** (leaves = nodes with two children + 1)
- A binary tree with n nodes has **n + 1 NULL links** and n − 1 edges
- Number of distinct binary tree shapes with n nodes = Catalan: 1, 2, **5**, 14, 42
- **Full/strict**: every node has 0 or 2 children; **complete**: all levels full except possibly the last, filled left to right; **perfect**: all leaves at the same level
- Array storage (0-based): children of i at **2i + 1** and **2i + 2**, parent at ⌊(i − 1)/2⌋ (1-based: 2i, 2i + 1, ⌊i/2⌋)

## Traversals – worked example
```
            A
          /   \
         B     C
        / \     \
       D   E     F
          /
         G
```
| Traversal | Rule | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Preorder | root, left, right | **A B D E G C F** |
| Inorder | left, root, right | **D B G E A C F** |
| Postorder | left, right, root | **D G E B F C A** |
| Level order (BFS, queue) | level by level | **A B C D E F G** |
- Inorder + preorder (or inorder + postorder) determines a unique tree; preorder + postorder does not (unless the tree is full)
- Rebuild: the first preorder (last postorder) symbol is the root; split the inorder at it

## Binary search tree (BST)
Left subtree < node < right subtree; **inorder gives sorted order**.
Insert 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80, 35:
```
             50
          /      \
        30        70
       /  \      /  \
      20   40   60   80
          /
         35
```
- Preorder 50 30 20 40 35 70 60 80 · Postorder 20 35 40 30 60 80 70 50 · height 3
- Search/insert/delete O(h): O(log n) when balanced, **O(n) when skewed** (sorted input makes a chain)
- Delete: leaf → remove; one child → link the child up; two children → replace with the **inorder successor** (smallest in the right subtree) or predecessor, then delete that node
- Delete 30 above → successor 35 takes its place

## Expression trees
Leaves are operands, internal nodes operators: (a + b) * c → root *, left +(a, b), right c. Preorder = prefix, inorder = infix, postorder = postfix.

## Balanced trees
- **AVL**: balance factor = height(left) − height(right) ∈ {−1, 0, 1}; fix with LL, RR (single) or LR, RL (double) rotations
- Inserting 10, 20, 30 into an AVL tree → RR case → rotate left → 20 is the root
- Others: red-black tree, B-tree / B+ tree (databases, multi-way), splay tree; **heap** = complete binary tree with the heap property
- **Threaded binary tree**: NULL links point to inorder predecessor/successor → traversal without a stack

## Traps
- Height vs depth vs level: read whether the root is counted as 0 or 1
- Inorder of a BST is sorted; preorder is not
- A complete binary tree is not necessarily full, and vice versa
- Level order needs a **queue**; recursive DFS traversals use a **stack**

notes.title: KRIES syllabus word by word – Binary trees
notes.md:
> **Syllabus:** Binary trees, sequential and linked representation, insertion and deletion on binary trees, binary tree traversal

### Binary trees
- **Means:** a tree in which every node has **at most two** children (left and right).
- **Key facts:** max nodes at level l = 2ˡ; max nodes with height h = 2ʰ⁺¹ − 1; leaves n₀ = n₂ + 1; n nodes → n + 1 NULL links; full, complete, perfect, skewed binary trees; distinct shapes with 3 nodes = 5.
- **Example:** expression (a + b) × c as a tree with × at the root.
- **Exam point:** a binary tree of height 3 has at most 15 nodes.

### Sequential representation
- **Means:** storing a binary tree in an **array**.
- **Key facts:** root at index 1 → children of i at **2i** and **2i + 1**, parent at ⌊i/2⌋ (0-based: 2i + 1, 2i + 2, ⌊(i − 1)/2⌋); efficient for complete trees (heaps); wasteful for skewed trees (height h needs 2ʰ⁺¹ − 1 cells).
- **Example:** A(1), B(2), C(3), D(4), E(5) → children of B are D and E.
- **Exam point:** a right-skewed tree of 4 nodes needs 15 array cells.

### Linked representation
- **Means:** each node = data + left pointer + right pointer.
- **Key facts:** `struct tnode { int data; struct tnode *left, *right; };`; no wasted cells; root pointer; parent pointer optional.
- **Example:** leaf: left = right = NULL.
- **Exam point:** n nodes have 2n pointers, of which n − 1 are used and n + 1 are NULL.

### Insertion on binary trees
- **Means:** adding a node.
- **Key facts:** general binary tree: insert at the first free position in level order (keeps it complete); **binary search tree**: compare with root, go left if smaller, right if larger, attach at a NULL link – O(h).
- **Example:** BST insert 50, 30, 70, 20, 40 → 30 and 70 children of 50; 20, 40 under 30.
- **Exam point:** inserting sorted data into a BST makes a skewed tree (O(n)).

### Deletion on binary trees
- **Means:** removing a node while keeping the tree valid.
- **Key facts:** BST: **leaf** → remove; **one child** → link the child to the parent; **two children** → replace with the **inorder successor** (smallest in right subtree) or predecessor, then delete that one. General tree: replace with the deepest-rightmost node, delete that.
- **Example:** delete 30 (children 20, 40) → 40 replaces 30 (if 40 has no left child).
- **Exam point:** the inorder successor has no left child.

### Binary tree traversal
- **Means:** visiting every node exactly once.
- **Key facts:** **preorder** (root, left, right), **inorder** (left, root, right), **postorder** (left, right, root), **level order** (queue); recursive ones use a stack; each O(n).
- **Example:** tree A(B(D, E(G)), C(–, F)): pre A B D E G C F · in D B G E A C F · post D G E B F C A · level A B C D E F G.
- **Exam point:** inorder of a BST is **sorted**; inorder + preorder rebuilds a unique tree.

### Q1. Rebuild from preorder ABDHEICFG and inorder HDBIEAFCG
- Preorder's first letter A is the root; inorder splits into HDBIE (left) and FCG (right)
- Left: preorder B D H E I → root B; inorder HD | IE → D has left child H; E has left child I
- Right: preorder C F G → root C, left F, right G
→ **Postorder H D I E B F G C A**, level order **A B C D E F G H I**, height **3**

### Q2. Rebuild from postorder DEBFCA and inorder DBEAFC
Root A (last of postorder) → left DBE (root B with D, E), right FC (root C with left F) → **preorder A B D E C F**

### Q3. BST from 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80
- Inorder 20 30 40 50 60 70 80 (sorted); search 60 → 50 → 70 → 60 (3 comparisons)
- Delete 50 (two children) → replace with the inorder successor **60** → root 60
- Delete 30 → successor 40 replaces it

### Q4. Max-heap by inserting 15, 10, 20, 8, 25, 5 one by one
15 → [15]; 10 → [15, 10]; 20 → swaps with 15 → [20, 10, 15]; 8 → [20, 10, 15, 8]; 25 → up past 10 and 20 → [25, 20, 15, 8, 10]; 5 → **[25, 20, 15, 8, 10, 5]**
Delete max → move 5 to the root and sift down → **[20, 10, 15, 8, 5]**

### Q5. Counts
- Binary tree with 20 leaves → nodes with two children = **19**
- Complete binary tree with 100 nodes → height ⌊log₂ 100⌋ = **6**, leaves = ⌈100/2⌉ = **50**
- Distinct binary trees with 4 nodes = Catalan(4) = **14**
- Array storage (1-based): parent of node 13 = 6, children of 6 = 12 and 13

notes.md:
## Concepts
- G = (V, E); directed/undirected, weighted, simple, multigraph (parallel edges), self-loop; path, cycle, connected, component, tree (connected, acyclic, n − 1 edges)
- Degree sum = 2E; max edges: undirected V(V − 1)/2 (K₅ = 10), directed V(V − 1)

## Representation
| | Adjacency matrix | Adjacency list |
|---|---|---|
| Space | O(V²) | O(V + E) |
| Edge test | O(1) | O(degree) |
| Best for | dense graphs | sparse graphs |
- Undirected matrix is symmetric; row sum = out-degree, column sum = in-degree; weighted: ∞ for no edge
- Lists hold 2E nodes (undirected) or E nodes (directed); also incidence matrix, edge list, multilist

## Traversals – O(V + E) with lists, O(V²) with a matrix
- BFS: queue, level by level, shortest paths in unweighted graphs, BFS tree has V − 1 edges
- DFS: stack/recursion, go deep, back edges show cycles; used for components, topological sort, cycle detection
- Example 1–2, 1–3, 2–4, 3–4, 4–5 from 1: BFS 1 2 3 4 5; DFS 1 2 4 3 5
- Weighted shortest paths: Dijkstra (min priority queue) – GPS

notes.title: Graphs – detailed notes with worked examples
notes.md:
## Terms
- G = (V, E); directed/undirected; weighted; **degree** (in-degree, out-degree); path, cycle, connected, strongly connected (directed), complete graph, tree (connected, acyclic, n − 1 edges), spanning tree, DAG
- **Σ degrees = 2|E|** (handshake lemma) → the number of odd-degree vertices is even
- Maximum edges: undirected n(n − 1)/2, directed n(n − 1)
- Complete graph Kₙ has **nⁿ⁻²** spanning trees (Cayley): K₄ → 16

## Representations
| | Adjacency matrix | Adjacency list |
|---|---|---|
| Space | O(V²) | O(V + E) |
| Edge (u, v)? | O(1) | O(degree) |
| All neighbours | O(V) | O(degree) |
| Best for | dense graphs | sparse graphs |
- Undirected matrix is symmetric; row sum = degree; incidence matrix is V × E

## BFS and DFS – worked example
Edges: A–B, A–C, B–D, B–E, C–F, E–F (neighbours in alphabetical order, start at A)
- **BFS** (queue): **A B C D E F** – visits level by level; gives shortest paths in an unweighted graph
- **DFS** (stack / recursion): **A B D E F C** – goes deep first, backtracks
- Both O(V + E) with lists, O(V²) with a matrix
- Uses: BFS – shortest path (unweighted), level order, broadcasting; DFS – cycle detection, topological sort, connected components, maze solving

## Minimum spanning tree – worked example
Edges (weight): A–B 4, A–C 2, B–C 1, B–D 5, C–D 8, C–E 10, D–E 2, D–F 6, E–F 3
- **Kruskal** (sort edges, add if no cycle – union–find): B–C 1, A–C 2, D–E 2, E–F 3, B–D 5 → **total 13** (A–B 4 rejected: cycle)
- **Prim** from A (grow one tree, cheapest edge leaving it): A–C 2, C–B 1, B–D 5, D–E 2, E–F 3 → **total 13**
- Same total; Kruskal O(E log E) good for sparse; Prim O(E log V) with a heap, O(V²) with a matrix, good for dense
- MST has V − 1 edges; unique if all weights are distinct

## Shortest paths
- **Dijkstra** (non-negative weights, greedy): from A on the graph above, final order A 0, C 2, B 3 (via C), D 8, E 10, F 13
- Bellman–Ford: negative weights allowed, detects negative cycles, O(VE)
- Floyd–Warshall: all pairs, O(V³), dynamic programming; Warshall: transitive closure

## Topological sort (DAG only)
Linear order with every edge u → v having u before v: repeatedly remove a vertex of in-degree 0 (Kahn), or reverse DFS finishing order. Used for task scheduling, course prerequisites, build systems. A graph with a cycle has none.

## Traps
- BFS uses a queue, DFS a stack
- Dijkstra fails with negative edge weights
- A tree with n vertices has exactly n − 1 edges; adding any edge makes a cycle
- Adjacency matrix of an undirected graph is symmetric, of a directed graph usually not

notes.title: KRIES syllabus word by word – Graphs
notes.md:
> **Syllabus:** Concepts, sequential and linked representation of graphs, BFS and DFS traversal

### Concepts
- **Means:** G = (V, E) – vertices joined by edges; models networks.
- **Key facts:** directed/undirected, weighted, degree (in/out), path, cycle, connected graph, complete graph (n(n − 1)/2 edges), tree = connected acyclic graph with n − 1 edges; Σ degree = 2|E|.
- **Example:** cities (vertices) and roads (edges).
- **Exam point:** an undirected graph with 6 vertices has at most 15 edges.

### Sequential representation (adjacency matrix)
- **Means:** an n × n matrix with A[i][j] = 1 (or the weight) if edge i–j exists.
- **Key facts:** space **O(V²)**; edge check O(1); symmetric for undirected graphs; row sum = degree (out-degree for directed); good for **dense** graphs.
- **Example:** edges A–B, A–C → row A: 0 1 1.
- **Exam point:** a graph with V vertices always needs V² cells, however few edges.

### Linked representation (adjacency list)
- **Means:** an array of lists – each vertex lists its neighbours.
- **Key facts:** space **O(V + E)**; listing neighbours is fast; edge check O(degree); good for **sparse** graphs; undirected edge appears in two lists.
- **Example:** A → B → C; B → A → D → E.
- **Exam point:** total list nodes = 2E (undirected) or E (directed).

### BFS traversal
- **Means:** breadth-first search – visit a vertex, then all its neighbours, then their neighbours (level by level).
- **Key facts:** uses a **queue** and a visited array; O(V + E) with lists; finds shortest paths (fewest edges) in unweighted graphs; gives a BFS tree.
- **Example:** edges A–B, A–C, B–D, B–E, C–F, E–F, start A → **A B C D E F**.
- **Exam point:** BFS ↔ level-order traversal of a tree.

### DFS traversal
- **Means:** depth-first search – go as deep as possible along one path, then backtrack.
- **Key facts:** uses a **stack** (or recursion); O(V + E); used for cycle detection, topological sort, connected components, maze solving.
- **Example:** same graph from A (neighbours in alphabetical order) → **A B D E F C**.
- **Exam point:** DFS ↔ preorder traversal of a tree.

notes.md:
## Searching
- Linear: unsorted OK; best 1, worst n, average (n + 1)/2 comparisons; O(n)
- Binary: sorted array; mid = low + (high − low)/2; worst ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 comparisons; O(log n); T(n) = T(n/2) + 1
- Hashing O(1) average (best), then binary, then linear

## Sorting
| Sort | Best | Average | Worst | Stable | In-place |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bubble (flag) | n | n² | n² | yes | yes |
| Selection | n² | n² | n² | no | yes |
| Insertion | n | n² | n² | yes | yes |
| Quick | n log n | n log n | n² | no | yes |
| Merge | n log n | n log n | n log n | yes | no (O(n)) |
| Heap | n log n | n log n | n log n | no | yes |
- Bubble: largest element moves to the end each pass; selection: n(n − 1)/2 comparisons, ≤ n − 1 swaps; insertion: shifts = inversions, best for nearly sorted data
- Quick sort: divide and conquer, pivot partition; worst case on sorted input with first/last pivot; merge sort least dependent on input order
- Lower bound for comparison sorts Ω(n log n); counting/radix sorts beat it for small integer keys

notes.title: Searching and sorting – detailed notes with worked examples
notes.md:
## Linear vs binary search
- Linear: any order; best 1, worst n, average (n + 1)/2 comparisons → O(n)
- **Binary**: sorted array only; O(log n); max comparisons ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 (1000 items → 10)

Binary search on [3, 8, 15, 23, 42, 56, 71, 89, 94] (indices 0–8):
| Find 71 | low | high | mid | a[mid] |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 8 | 4 | 42 < 71 → low = 5 |
| 2 | 5 | 8 | 6 | **71 found** (2 comparisons) |
| Find 10 | 0 → 0 → 2 | 8 → 3 → 3 | 4, 1, 2 | 42, 8, 15 → low 2 > high 1: **not found** |

## Sorting passes on [64, 25, 12, 22, 11]
**Bubble** (largest sinks to the end each pass):
1. 25 12 22 11 **64** 2. 12 22 11 **25 64** 3. 12 11 **22 25 64** 4. **11 12 22 25 64**

**Selection** (find the minimum, swap into place):
1. **11** 25 12 22 64 2. 11 **12** 25 22 64 3. 11 12 **22** 25 64 4. 11 12 22 25 64

**Insertion** (insert the next item into the sorted left part):
1. 25 64 | 12 22 11 2. 12 25 64 | 22 11 3. 12 22 25 64 | 11 4. 11 12 22 25 64

## Quick sort – Lomuto partition, pivot = last
[10, 80, 30, 90, 40, 50, 70], pivot 70 → elements < 70 move left → **[10, 30, 40, 50, 70, 90, 80]**, pivot at index 4; recurse on both sides
- Best/average O(n log n); **worst O(n²)** when the pivot is always the smallest/largest (already sorted input with first/last pivot); not stable; in-place

## Merge sort
Split in halves until size 1, merge sorted halves: [38, 27, 43, 3] → [27, 38] [3, 43] → [3, 27, 38, 43]. Always O(n log n), stable, needs O(n) extra space.

## Heap sort
Build a max-heap, swap the root with the last element, shrink, heapify. Max-heap of [1, 3, 5, 4, 6, 13, 10, 9, 8, 15, 17] → [17, 15, 13, 9, 6, 5, 10, 4, 8, 3, 1]. O(n log n) always, in-place, not stable.

## Summary table
| Algorithm | Best | Average | Worst | Space | Stable |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bubble | O(n)* | O(n²) | O(n²) | O(1) | yes |
| Selection | O(n²) | O(n²) | O(n²) | O(1) | no |
| Insertion | O(n) | O(n²) | O(n²) | O(1) | yes |
| Merge | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | O(n) | yes |
| Quick | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | O(n²) | O(log n) | no |
| Heap | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | O(1) | no |
| Counting / Radix | O(n + k) / O(d(n + k)) | | | O(n + k) | yes |
\* bubble sort with a "no swaps → stop" flag. Selection sort makes the **fewest swaps** (n − 1). Insertion sort is best for nearly sorted data. Comparison sorts cannot beat **Ω(n log n)**.

## Hashing
- h(k) = k mod m (division method); collisions resolved by **chaining** (lists) or **open addressing**: linear probing (h + i), quadratic probing (h + i²), double hashing
- Insert 23, 43, 13, 27, 37, 50 into a table of 10 with linear probing:
  23 → 3; 43 → 3 taken → **4**; 13 → 3, 4 taken → **5**; 27 → 7; 37 → 7 taken → **8**; 50 → 0
  Final: [50, –, –, 23, 43, 13, –, 27, 37, –]
- Load factor α = n/m; linear probing suffers **primary clustering**, quadratic **secondary clustering**
- Average search O(1); worst O(n)

## Traps
- Binary search needs a **sorted** array and random access
- Number of passes for bubble/selection = n − 1
- Quick sort's worst case is O(n²) even though it is "quick"
- Stable = equal keys keep their original order

> **Syllabus:** Linear and binary search; selection, insertion, quick and merge sort

### Linear search
- **Means:** check elements one by one from the start until found.
- **Key facts:** works on unsorted data and linked lists; best 1 comparison, worst n, average (n + 1)/2 → O(n).
- **Example:** find 7 in [4, 9, 7, 1] → found at the 3rd comparison.
- **Exam point:** the only choice for unsorted, unindexed data.

### Binary search
- **Means:** on a **sorted** array, compare with the middle and discard half each time.
- **Key facts:** mid = (low + high)/2; O(log n); max comparisons ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 (1024 items → 11); needs random access (not linked lists).
- **Example:** [3, 8, 15, 23, 42, 56, 71, 89, 94], find 71 → mid 42 → right half → mid 71 found (2 comparisons).
- **Exam point:** `low + (high − low)/2` avoids integer overflow.

### Selection sort
- **Means:** repeatedly select the **minimum** of the unsorted part and swap it to the front.
- **Key facts:** n − 1 passes; n(n − 1)/2 comparisons always → O(n²) in every case; at most n − 1 swaps (fewest swaps); not stable; in-place.
- **Example:** 64 25 12 22 11 → 11 25 12 22 64 → 11 12 25 22 64 → 11 12 22 25 64.
- **Exam point:** best when swaps (writes) are expensive.

### Insertion sort
- **Means:** take the next element and insert it into its place in the sorted left part (like arranging cards).
- **Key facts:** best O(n) (already sorted), worst O(n²) (reverse sorted); stable; in-place; online (works as data arrives); good for small or nearly sorted lists.
- **Example:** 64 25 12 22 11 → 25 64 | … → 12 25 64 | … → 12 22 25 64 | 11 → 11 12 22 25 64.
- **Exam point:** number of shifts = number of inversions.

### Quick sort
- **Means:** divide and conquer – choose a **pivot**, partition into smaller-than and larger-than parts, sort each part recursively (C. A. R. Hoare, 1960).
- **Key facts:** average/best O(n log n); **worst O(n²)** (sorted input with first/last pivot); not stable; in-place; O(log n) stack on average; Lomuto and Hoare partition schemes.
- **Example:** [10, 80, 30, 90, 40, 50, 70], pivot 70 → [10, 30, 40, 50, **70**, 90, 80].
- **Exam point:** after one partition the pivot is in its **final** position.

### Merge sort
- **Means:** divide and conquer – split into halves, sort each, **merge** the sorted halves (John von Neumann, 1945).
- **Key facts:** O(n log n) in every case; T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n; **stable**; needs O(n) extra space; best for linked lists and external sorting.
- **Example:** [38, 27, 43, 3] → [27, 38] + [3, 43] → [3, 27, 38, 43].
- **Exam point:** merging two sorted lists of sizes m and n takes at most m + n − 1 comparisons.

notes.title: Solved exam problems – counting comparisons and passes
notes.md:
### Q1. Binary search on 1000 sorted items
Maximum comparisons = ⌊log₂ 1000⌋ + 1 = **10**; for 1024 items → 11; linear search worst case 1000, average ≈ 500.

### Q2. Binary search trace
[3, 8, 15, 23, 42, 56, 71, 89, 94]: search 23 → mid index 4 (42) → left half 0–3, mid 1 (8) → right 2–3, mid 2 (15) → right 3–3, mid 3 (23) found → **4 comparisons**

### Q3. Bubble sort counts
n = 6 → passes 5, comparisons 15 (n(n − 1)/2); already sorted with the swap flag → 1 pass, 5 comparisons. Reverse-sorted 5 elements → 10 swaps.

### Q4. Insertion sort shifts = number of inversions
[3, 1, 2] has inversions (3,1), (3,2) → **2 shifts**; [5, 4, 3, 2, 1] → 10.

### Q5. Selection sort swaps
At most n − 1 = 4 swaps for 5 elements – the fewest of the simple sorts.

### Q6. Quick sort partition
[10, 80, 30, 90, 40, 50, 70], pivot 70 (last) → [10, 30, 40, 50, **70**, 90, 80]; worst case on sorted input: n(n − 1)/2 = 21 comparisons for 7 items.

### Q7. Merge sort
Merging [3, 27, 38] and [9, 43, 82] → 3, 9, 27, 38, 43, 82 with at most 3 + 3 − 1 = **5** comparisons; merge sort on 8 items needs 3 levels (log₂ 8).

### Q8. Which sort?
Nearly sorted data → insertion; stable O(n log n) → merge; in-place O(n log n) worst case → heap; fastest on average in practice → quick; fewest writes → selection.
